question.text: Activist Strategy (or Special Situations Strategy) Cat III AIFs differ from traditional Cat III funds because they:

answer.text: Have a less diversified portfolio with illiquid investments, and take a long-term PE-style approach to investee companies
Have a more diversified portfolio with liquid holdings
Invest only in listed Nifty-50 index constituents
Are prohibited from voting in investee company matters

explanation.text: The Logic: Per the AIF Managers workbook on Activist/Special Situations strategy (pp. 279-280), activist Category III AIFs take a private-equity and long-term oriented approach to their investee companies, may target companies undergoing NCLT proceedings, and are expected to monitor and vote on important matters. They differ from traditional Category III funds because they have less diversified portfolios and hold illiquid investments. The Trap: A more diversified portfolio with liquid holdings describes traditional Category III long-short strategies, not activist funds. Activist funds are not restricted to Nifty-50 constituents in the source. Activist Category III funds are expected to vote on important matters, not prohibited from voting. Note: The source on pp. 279-280 anchors the activist Category III definition on the PE-like, long-term, less diversified, illiquid-investment approach combined with active monitoring and voting on investee company matters.
